$comment: Why two published packages describe one thing differently, read by scripts/check_label_agreement.py. It sits beside registry.json rather than inside a package because no single descriptor can own a statement about two of them. EACH ENTRY PINS THE VALUES IT EXCUSES, and that is the whole mechanism: a reason closes ONE difference between THESE values, so a package moving one of them makes the entry stop matching, the check exits 1 as a stale reason, and the difference is reported again. An entry that named only the label would be a standing licence to disagree about it forever, which is silencing the check with extra steps. An entry with no `reason` sentence is refused outright. Nothing here is written by a script — a check that can write its own exemptions can be silenced by running it. Differences absent from this file are OPEN: the check prints them on every run with the entry that would close them, and does not fail, because two packages may legitimately differ where their populations differ and no check can know which. `corrections` is the OPPOSITE list and it closes nothing. A reason says a difference is legitimate; a correction says it is a defect, names the side that is wrong, the value it must become and the act that lands the fix — and the difference goes on being reported and `--strict` goes on failing on it. That asymmetry is the whole mechanism: a correction that closed a difference would be a reason with a different word on it, and a bug excused by a sentence. What it buys is that the answer is written where the check can hold it to the packages: each entry pins a declaration by a `pointer` addressed by NAME rather than by index, so it reddens when the declaration moves AND when the fix arrives, and it can be deleted only by the thing being true. It reaches declarations the comparison never sees — a description, a join's cardinality — because the instances this file has to account for do not all live in the space between two constraints. A CORRECTION IS BLOCKED ON AN ACT THIS REPOSITORY CANNOT MAKE ALONE: a descriptor is stamped into the Parquet footer of the object it describes and declares that object's sha256, so changing a published declaration is a republish and not an edit, and a surface in another repository is changed there. That is why a verdict is recorded rather than applied. An empty `corrections` list means no verdict is outstanding.

reasons.reason: The GLEIF register types these elements differently and this label is coarser than that distinction. LEI-CDF v3.1 types `country` as CountryCodeType, a two-letter code and nothing else, and `jurisdiction` as JurisdictionCodeType, a union of CountryCodeType and RegionCodeType which admits country-hyphen-subdivision (US-DE, AE-SH). `edgar_gleif.jurisdiction` is that same `jurisdiction` element carried through the join, declared `geography.location.country_code` in its package's nominations.finetype.json because no label names the union, and it declares the same union pattern as `gleif.jurisdiction`. Each pattern is the shape its own element is typed to, the descriptions in both descriptors say so, and making `country` agree with the two `jurisdiction` columns would mean one of them lying about the register it came from. Note the direction for a reader validating all three: every value `country` admits, both `jurisdiction` columns admit too.

The populations differ and the patterns are each true of their own. `edgar` carries a ticker for every security in the SEC company-tickers file; `edgar_gleif` carries only the subset that resolved to an LEI. The four-letter-plus-period form occurs in the EDGAR column and `edgar.ticker` is widened to admit it — its `x-finetype-pattern-fit` records the widening against finetype's canonical pattern — while the crosswalk snapshot contains no such value and declares the canonical pattern unwidened. So `edgar`'s pattern is the union of the two: a validation routine written against it passes both datasets, and one written against `edgar_gleif`'s narrower pattern fails on EDGAR rows. That asymmetry is the thing worth knowing, and it is why this is recorded rather than closed by widening `edgar_gleif` — a pattern wider than its own column would be less true of the bytes it describes, and changing it would need a republish of the object whose footer carries this descriptor.

Two register elements under one label, each with its own bounds. `edgar.company_name` and `edgar_gleif.company_name` are the SEC display name of a registrant, declared `representation.text.entity_name` in each package's nominations.finetype.json, and they carry that label's own bounds of 2 to 200 characters, which the descriptor check holds every value in both columns to. `gleif.legal_name` and `edgar_gleif.legal_name` are the GLEIF register's legal-name element, which LEI-CDF v3.1 types as Tokenized500Type, 1 to 500 characters; single-character and longer-than-200-character names are genuinely registered, so those two columns carry the register's bounds rather than the label's, and both descriptors say so. The direction for a reader validating all four: the register's bounds admit every company name, and the label's bounds would refuse real register names.
